title: Knowledge Check 6: Lessons 41-50
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 41-50 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Case Study: Research & Summarization Agents", what is the thesis that explains the architecture?
options: A research agent is a token-scaling machine whose accuracy is bounded by how faithfully it can compress many sources into one brief without losing the source of each claim
A research agent is a support agent with broader search tools
A research agent should compress as aggressively as possible and drop citations for speed
A research agent's accuracy is bounded only by the size of its context window
questions.explanation: The lesson states that everything in the design, the subagents, the memory, the citation verifier, exists to stop a fluent summary from outrunning the evidence it quotes.

questions.question: Why does the lesson say research needs an agent rather than a workflow?
options: Because the public web is too large to index
Because research is open-ended and the required steps cannot be predicted in advance, so the plan is the output of the first few searches
Because retrieval quality is worse than in support work
Because citations always require a human reviewer
questions.explanation: The lesson applies the workflow-versus-agent distinction and names research as the clearest case for the agent end of the spectrum, because no one can write the plan in advance and the investigation is path-dependent.

questions.question: Which architecture does the lesson describe for the research system?
options: A single agent with one web search tool looping until it stops
A fixed workflow over a predefined list of sources
An orchestrator-worker pattern where a lead agent coordinates specialized subagents that run in parallel with their own context windows and search tasks
A debate between two agents that argue until they agree
questions.explanation: The lesson describes the shipped system as a lead researcher coordinating specialized subagents that run in parallel, each with its own context window and search task.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Case Study: Workflow Automation Agents (Browsers, Clicks, and Typing)", what is the one idea to carry out?
options: The model's reasoning rarely fails: grounding fails when the click lands on the wrong element, and blast radius is underestimated when the click submits something real, and both are engineering problems solved before production
Better prompting is the main fix for click accuracy
Screenshots are the only reliable way for an agent to observe a page
Rules-based automation should be replaced entirely by agents
questions.explanation: The lesson states plainly that both failure modes in this class are engineering problems rather than prompting problems, and that both get solved before the agent ever runs in production.

questions.question: The lesson does arithmetic on per-step reliability for a multi-step job. What conclusion does it draw?
options: A per-step success rate of 90 percent is fine for long jobs because errors cancel out
A 90 percent per-step success rate collapses across many steps, so steps should be collapsed into verified atomic commands and checked after each one
Per-step rates are irrelevant because agents retry until they succeed
Longer jobs are safer because the agent gets more chances to correct itself
questions.explanation: The lesson walks the arithmetic showing a high per-step rate collapsing across ten steps, and prescribes collapsing work into verified atomic commands with a check after each one.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what makes this class of agent carry risks no other class does?
options: It needs a larger context window than text-only agents
It cannot be traced with standard observability tooling
A page is hostile input, and every action lands directly in a production system
It requires a human to execute every step
questions.explanation: The lesson names those two risks specifically: the page can be adversarial input, and the agent's actions land in live systems rather than in a sandbox.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Case Study: Coding Agents (Hermes, Claude Code, and Copilot Under the Hood)", what does a coding agent have that the browser agent from the previous case study did not?
options: A verifier that runs itself, because a test, build, or linter returns a pass or fail the agent can read in the same conversation
A larger model with a longer context window
A human reviewer standing by for every step
A cheaper per-token API contract
questions.explanation: The lesson says the one idea to carry out is that a coding agent gets a verifier that runs itself, which changes both the reliability math and what done means, and contrasts it with the browser agent that needed external verification.

questions.question: The lesson places coding assistants on a spectrum. Which description matches the cloud agent rung?
options: Ghost text after the cursor that you accept with one key press
An agent that works in a background ephemeral environment, runs tests and linters there, and hands back a pull request to review
An agent that edits your local working tree only after you approve each file
A chat window that explains code without touching any files
questions.explanation: The lesson describes Copilot's cloud agent as working in the background in its own ephemeral development environment, executing tests and linters and opening a pull request, with the blast radius contained to a reviewable diff.

questions.question: What does the lesson say about the harness?
options: The harness is the model itself, and tools are optional extras
The harness is a second model that reviews the first model's edits
The model alone can only emit text; the harness supplies the tools, context management, and execution environment that make it a coding agent
The harness is a fixed program whose behavior cannot be extended
questions.explanation: The lesson quotes the docs describing the harness as the layer providing tools, context management, and execution environment, and adds that tools are what make the model agentic and the tool surface is where capability is extended.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Enterprise Integration: Connecting Agents to Salesforce, ERP, CRM, and Data Warehouses", what is the first design decision when connecting an agent to a system of record?
options: Which SDK or API endpoint to use for the connection
Whether the call is a read or a write, because reads and writes need different identities, permissions, and guardrails
Which cloud region the system runs in
Whether to use a direct API or a managed platform
Which LLM provider to route the tool call through
questions.explanation: The lesson says to separate the read path from the write path first, because reading accepts a narrower identity and smaller blast radius while writing changes live business data. The connection mechanism is the small part; identity and reversibility come first.

questions.question: What does the lesson cite from Snowflake's managed MCP server documentation as the recommended way to expose warehouse data to an agent on the read path?
options: Expose a raw SQL execution tool so the agent has full query freedom
Expose the managed MCP server together with the SQL execution tool on the same server so they share permissions
Expose a Cortex Agent as the client-facing tool, keeping the agent inside semantic views and verified queries, and isolate any direct SQL behind a separate least-privileged role
Always disable all MCP tools and expose the warehouse through a direct REST API only
Store the data in the agent's own vector store instead of querying the warehouse
questions.explanation: The Snowflake docs recommend exposing a Cortex Agent as the governed client-facing tool, and warn that exposing the SQL execution tool on the same server lets a client bypass the agent's semantic views, verified queries, and orchestration. If direct SQL is required it should be on a separate server with a dedicated least-privileged role.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what is the key difference between the write path into a CRM and the read path into a data warehouse?
options: The write path never needs a least-privileged role because writes are performed inside the CRM
Both paths always use the same shared identity and grants

The write path changes live business data, so it should prefer platform actions that apply business rules and put human confirmation on destructive or expensive operations, while reads stay read-only inside governed views
The write path should always use a direct API while the read path must always use MCP
The write path requires a higher recursion depth than the read path
questions.explanation: The lesson stresses that a write is a commitment in shared state and should go through governed platform actions with a human confirmation at the blast-radius boundary, while the read path stays read-only inside the warehouse's own governance. The two paths use separate identities, separate grants, and separate guardrails.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Vector DB Operations: Scaling, Backups, Consistency, and Cost", what is the real variable that decides whether a pgvector HNSW index is fast?
options: The number of shards the collection is split across
Whether the index working set fits in memory, because HNSW traversal is a chain of random accesses and disk reads degrade latency by an order of magnitude or more
The PostgreSQL connection pool size
The ANN index type chosen at creation
questions.explanation: The lesson states that HNSW search is a chain of random accesses through a graph and that the index must live in memory to be fast; when it spills to disk, query latency jumps 10 to 100 times. Row count is a proxy; memory is the variable.

questions.question: The lesson says a backup can meet the database RPO and still fail the retrieval RPO. What does that mean?
options: The database restore succeeded but the indexes were rebuilt with different ANN parameters
Rows were restored cleanly, but the retrieval system was not restored to a known semantic state, so search returns old chunks or mixes embedding model versions
The physical backup was taken before the last write was committed
The restore ran faster than the recovery time objective allowed
questions.explanation: The lesson's example: you restore the database cleanly, the application comes back, but support search returns old policy chunks and mixes two embedding model versions in the same result set. The backup met the database recovery point but failed the retrieval recovery point.

questions.question: The lesson argues that most teams have never declared a consistency model for their RAG pipeline. What is the stated consequence of that?
options: The system is strongly consistent by default because the vector index updates synchronously
The system is eventually consistent, implicitly, with a staleness bound nobody measured and no monitoring to detect when the actual window exceeds the intended one
The inconsistency window is zero because the source of truth is the vector database
Consistency only matters for relational data, not for vector search
questions.explanation: The lesson says the absence of a declaration is not the absence of a model; it is an implicit model: your system is eventually consistent, designed by nobody, with a staleness bound nobody measured and no monitoring to catch when the real window exceeds the intended one.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Data Pipelines for RAG: ETL, Connectors, CDC, and Incremental Refresh”, what is the central focus?
options: Connectors (pull versus push), normalizing data before it hits the embedding model, change data capture as the mechanism that turns a polling job into a live one, and incremental refresh that re-embeds only the records that changed.
A history of vector database vendors and their pricing tiers
A review of unrelated content management tools
A summary of corporate governance policies
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: Connectors (pull versus push), normalizing data before it hits the embedding model, change data capture as the mechanism that turns a polling job into a live one, and incremental refresh that re-embeds only the records that changed.

questions.question: Why does the lesson say a RAG pipeline must normalize data before it reaches the embedding model?
options: Because normalization is a nice-to-have that only matters for very large corpora
Because raw payloads contain structure and noise that waste the embedding token budget, dilute attention with recurring system strings, and produce low-quality vectors that retrieve poorly
Because normalization replaces the need for chunking entirely
Because the embedding model can automatically separate signal from syntax on its own
questions.explanation: The lesson states that raw SaaS JSON and raw HTML are hostile to vector retrieval: embedding them wastes tokens on structural syntax, causes the model to assign weight to recurring system strings instead of meaning, and yields low-quality vectors.

questions.question: Which mechanism does the lesson describe as the reason change data capture enables incremental rather than sweeping updates?
options: CDC sends a stream of events for inserts, updates, and deletes, so the pipeline knows exactly which document changed and can re-embed only that content
CDC re-embeds the entire corpus on every run to guarantee consistency
CDC replaces the embedding model entirely
CDC requires polling the whole dataset more frequently
questions.explanation: Log-based CDC taps the source transaction log and emits an event for every insert, update, and delete, so the pipeline is told exactly what changed and can process only the affected records instead of re-embedding everything.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Building an Eval Program", why must the eval harness be consistent, and what is the main thing to pin to achieve it?
options: Pin the application prompt to keep example ordering fixed across runs
Pin the judge model snapshot and dataset version so a score difference reflects a quality change rather than measurement noise
Run the harness only on release candidates so it is never compared across environments
Use the newest model alias so the judge stays current each run
questions.explanation: The lesson says consistency is the harness's non-negotiable property: the same input must produce the same score so differences reflect quality change. It names an unpinned judge as the main culprit, since providers update models behind the same version name, and stresses pinning the judge snapshot and dataset version.

questions.question: How does the lesson say a capability eval becomes a regression eval?
options: A capability eval is deleted as soon as it passes so the suite stays small
A capability eval is refreshed from new production output each quarter
A capability eval that hits a persistently high pass rate graduates into the regression suite, where it starts measuring whether the behavior still works reliably
A capability eval is run only by human graders once it passes
questions.explanation: The lesson describes the self-healing structure: once an eval hits a persistently high pass rate it graduates from asking can we do this at all to asking can we still do this reliably, so nothing already proven can quietly regress.

questions.question: What cost discipline does the lesson say keeps an eval quality gate from being switched off?
options: Run the full LLM-as-judge suite on every commit to catch regressions early
Use cheap code-based graders in CI on every commit and reserve expensive LLM-as-judge evaluations for preview and production
Run no automated evals and rely on manual review of a few prompts before each release
Run expensive evals only on Fridays so the bill stays low
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that a gate costing real money on every commit gets switched off the first month, so it wires the cheap code-based layers into every-commit CI and reserves the expensive judges for preview and production evaluation.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Governance: AI Policies, Review Boards, and Model Risk Management”, what is the central focus?
options: Governance is the answer to three questions: who is allowed to change the agent, the model, or the data it touches, who gets to accept the risk when we ship anyway, and how we prove the decisions were made deliberately by someone with authority. Its three building blocks are policies, a review board, and model risk management.
Governance is a synonym for writing a single corporate policy document that covers every possible AI use case.
Governance is a technical feature that automatically rejects prompts that exceed a token limit before they reach the model.
Governance is a marketing term for making an AI product easier to demo to enterprise buyers.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that governance is the answer to three questions measurement cannot answer: who is allowed to change the agent, who gets to accept the risk when shipping anyway, and how the decisions are proven to have been made deliberately by an authorized party. Its building blocks are AI policies, a review board, and model risk management, which the lesson presents as the layer that decides, records, and proves.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance on a review board?
options: A review board should approve every AI use so no decision escapes oversight.
A review board should not approve every AI use, should not replace system owners, and should produce decisions, owners, deadlines, and records rather than only discussing risk.
A review board should be made up only of technologists so technical risk is fully understood.
A review board should replace the people who build, buy, own, and operate each AI system.
questions.explanation: The lesson gives three disciplines that keep a review board from becoming theater: it should not approve every AI use (that creates a bottleneck), it should not replace system owners (a named person stays accountable for each system), and a useful meeting produces decisions, owners, deadlines, and records rather than only discussing risk. A committee made of a single discipline, and a committee that does the building and owning, are presented as failures.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support about model risk management?
options: After the April 2026 replacement of SR 11-7 by SR 26-2, generative and agentic AI are carved out of supervisory scope, but the core discipline of inventory, tiering, independent validation, and ongoing monitoring still applies and must cover AI systems as models.
The US stopped requiring model risk management entirely in 2011, so AI systems no longer need any validation.
Model risk management applies only to banks and is irrelevant to how an enterprise decides which agents to run.
A model only needs to be validated once at launch and then requires no further monitoring because its risk profile never changes.
questions.explanation: The lesson confirms the April 2026 rescission of SR 11-7 in favor of SR 26-2 and notes that generative and agentic AI are excluded from the new guidance's scope, which means the hardest class of model must be governed by judgment for now. It then states the transferable core still holds for AI: inventory every system, tier by damage, validate high-risk systems independently, and monitor after deployment, since a model's risk profile changes as the world it operates in changes.

questions.question: Per the lesson on security architecture for AI, which two OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) risks drive the need to inspect AI traffic at the application layer?
options: Unbounded consumption and supply chain
Prompt injection and sensitive information disclosure
Data and model poisoning and misinformation
System prompt leakage and vector weaknesses
questions.explanation: The lesson names prompt injection, which tops the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) list, and sensitive information disclosure, which sits second, as the two application-layer problems that look like ordinary HTTP traffic. Both are why the perimeter alone is insufficient and layers must be stacked.

questions.question: Why should a web application firewall (WAF) not be treated as the only line of defense for an AI workload?
options: A WAF cannot enforce authentication or quotas on its own
A WAF reads the shape of requests, not their semantic meaning, so rephrased or encoded injections bypass string matching
A WAF costs more per evaluation than the model it protects
A WAF can only filter network traffic and never application-layer HTTP
questions.explanation: The lesson stresses that a WAF reads text, not meaning, so an attacker can bypass a phrase match by rephrasing, encoding the prompt, or using indirect injection. That is why the semantic guardrail at the application layer is a second trust boundary.

questions.question: Per the lesson, why must data loss prevention for AI operate at the interaction layer rather than only at file and email gateways?
options: Because AI data often leaks inside application-layer interactions such as prompts, tool calls, and model outputs, not as transferred files
Because email gateways cannot classify sensitive data at all
Because the perimeter has no place in an AI architecture
Because tool calls never carry sensitive data
questions.explanation: The lesson shows that AI introduces a new path: sensitive content is embedded in prompts, retrieved context, embeddings, tool calls, and model outputs. A policy enforced only at email and storage gateways lets the same data walk out through a chat prompt, so DLP must inspect the interaction itself.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Privacy: PII, Data Minimization, Retention, and Consent for AI", what is the one idea to carry out?
options: An agent that touches personal data is allowed to touch the least of it, for the shortest time, on a defensible legal basis, and the person concerned has to be able to tell what was done and stop it
Network security alone is enough to make an agent lawful
Collecting more context is always the way to make an agent smarter
Consent is the only lawful basis under the GDPR
questions.explanation: That is the lesson's central framing: the privacy layer decides which data the security layer even has to defend, and it rests on recognition, minimization, retention, and a real legal basis.

questions.question: The lesson says that context turns a neutral value into personal data. Which example does it give?
options: A customer ID with no accompanying information becomes personal data the moment the agent pulls the account record it points to
An email address is only personal data when a name appears right next to it
A customer ID is never personal data because it is a random string
Names and phone numbers are the only categories that count as personal data
questions.explanation: Lesson 50 makes the point explicitly: a customer ID looks like a random string on its own, but the moment the agent assembles the account record it points to, the combination relates to a person, so recognition must happen across assembled context, not field by field.

questions.question: According to the lesson, data minimization for the agent's tool interface means what?
options: The tool call should pass the specific identifier and the specific fields needed, not the entire object graph it has access to
Every tool should return the full record so the model never misses context
Minimization is a system prompt telling the model to only use necessary data
Breaking minimization, then adding it later, is the same as doing it up front
questions.explanation: Lesson 50 treats the tool interface as a minimization failure point: passing the whole customer row because the function happens to exist still puts data into context it did not need, and minimization belongs in the architecture, not the prompt.
